demosthenes#text: Demosthenes lost his father early and had to win his inheritance in court; according to tradition he overcame a speech impediment by speaking against the surf with pebbles in his mouth. As a politician he warned in his Philippics against the rise of Philip II of Macedon and forged an alliance with Thebes, which was defeated at Chaeronea in 338 BC. After Alexander's death he again called on the Greeks to revolt; when the Macedonians won, he took poison in 322 BC on the island of Calauria to escape capture. In antiquity his speeches were regarded as the standard of eloquence, and Cicero took him as a model.
euklid#summary: The mathematician from Alexandria whose Elements was the textbook of geometry for more than two thousand years.
euklid#text: Little is known about Euclid's life; he taught around 300 BC in Alexandria under Ptolemy I and is said to have answered the king's question about an easier route to mathematics by saying that there is no royal road. In the 13 books of the Elements he summarized the mathematical knowledge of his time and derived, step by step from a few definitions and axioms, all the propositions of geometry and number theory, among them the Pythagorean theorem and the proof that there are infinitely many prime numbers. This method of rigorous proof became the model for all science. The Elements was translated into Arabic and Latin and used as a school textbook into the 20th century.
archimedes#summary: The most important natural scientist of antiquity, discoverer of the law of the lever and of buoyancy.
archimedes#text: Archimedes lived in Syracuse on Sicily and was in contact with the scholars of Alexandria. He calculated the number pi with great accuracy, determined the areas and volumes of the sphere and the cylinder, and formulated the law of the lever and the principle of buoyancy named after him, which according to legend he discovered in the bathtub and celebrated with the cry Eureka. As an engineer he built pulley systems, the water screw for irrigation, and war machines to defend his city against the Romans. During the capture of Syracuse in 212 BC he was killed by a Roman soldier; his writings were preserved in the Middle Ages in Byzantium and in the Islamic world.
laozi#summary: The sage to whom the Daodejing is attributed and who is regarded as the counterpart and complement of Confucius.
laozi#text: According to tradition, Laozi, the old master, was an archivist at the Zhou court and an older contemporary of Confucius, who is said to have asked him for advice. When he left the crumbling empire, a border guard is said to have asked him to write down his wisdom, from which the Daodejing arose. Whether he really existed is unclear; scholarship dates the text to the 4th or 3rd century BC and holds it to be the work of several authors. As a deity of religious Daoism, Laozi was later venerated in temples, and the Tang emperors saw him as their ancestor.
sunzi#summary: The author of the Art of War, the oldest and still the most widely read textbook of strategy.
sunzi#text: Sun Wu, honorifically called Sunzi, served according to tradition as a general to the king of Wu in southeastern China and led his army to victories over the powerful state of Chu. His work in thirteen chapters deals with planning, deception, terrain, espionage, and the leading of soldiers, and teaches that the best victory is the one won without fighting. As with Laozi, his dates and authorship are disputed; the text probably comes from the period of the Warring States. The Art of War became required reading for officers throughout East Asia and is today also quoted in business and politics.
sima-qian#summary: The father of Chinese historiography, who completed his life's work, the Shiji, despite a severe punishment.
sima-qian#text: Sima Qian took over from his father Sima Tan the office of grand astrologer and archivist at the court of the Han emperor Wu, and with it the plan for a complete history of China. On journeys through the empire he collected traditions, questioned witnesses, and visited tombs and battlefields. Because he defended the general Li Ling against the emperor's anger, he was sentenced to castration in 99 BC; in a famous letter he explained why he endured the disgrace in order to finish his work. His vivid biographies of rulers, assassins, merchants, and scholars made the Shiji a masterpiece of literature as well.
wu-zetian#summary: The only woman who ruled China as empress in her own right, promoting the administration and Buddhism as she did so.
wu-zetian#text: Wu Zhao came to the court of Emperor Taizong at the age of fourteen as a concubine and, after his death, became the consort of his son Gaozong, whom she soon directed from behind the scenes. She removed rivals and opponents with severity, but governed effectively: she lowered the taxes of the peasants, expanded the civil service examinations, secured the borders, and had a huge Buddha statue created in the Longmen Grottoes that is said to bear her features. From 690 to 705 she ruled under a dynastic name of her own. Confucian historians later portrayed her as a cruel usurper, yet her reforms laid the ground for the flowering of the Tang in the 8th century.
murasaki-shikibu#summary: The author of the Tale of Genji, who with her work established the novel as a literary form.
murasaki-shikibu#text: Murasaki Shikibu came from a learned branch of the Fujiwara family and as a girl secretly studied the Chinese classics, which were properly reserved for men. After the early death of her husband she entered the service of Empress Shoshi around 1006, where she wrote her Tale of Genji and kept a diary about life at court. Her real name is unknown; Murasaki is the name of a character in the novel, and Shikibu refers to her father's office. Her novel about love, power, and transience at the imperial court is still read today and is regarded in Japan as a national epic.
kalidasa#summary: The greatest poet of Sanskrit literature, whose drama Shakuntala delighted even Goethe.
kalidasa#text: Kalidasa probably lived in the 4th or 5th century at the court of the Gupta kings, presumably under Chandragupta II; otherwise almost nothing is known about his life. His drama Shakuntala tells of a king's love for the daughter of a hermit, whom he forgets through a curse and finds again; the poem Meghaduta has a cloud carry messages of love across India. His works combine the depiction of nature, mythology, and a fine rendering of feeling in artful language. The first German translation of Shakuntala in 1791 set off enthusiasm for Indian poetry in Europe.
xuanzang#summary: The Buddhist monk who traveled for sixteen years through Central Asia and India and brought hundreds of scriptures back to China.
xuanzang#text: In 629 Xuanzang left China despite an imperial ban on travel, crossed deserts and mountain ranges, and studied for years at the monastic university of Nalanda in India. In 645 he returned to Chang'an with 657 scriptures, relics, and statues, where Emperor Taizong received him with honor and set up a translation workshop for him; the Great Wild Goose Pagoda was built to house the texts. His account of the western regions remains an important source for the history of India and Central Asia to this day. In the 16th century his journey became a popular legend in the novel Journey to the West, with the Monkey King.
paul-von-hindenburg#summary: Victor of Tannenberg, head of the Supreme Army Command, and, as Reich president, the man who appointed Hitler chancellor.
paul-von-hindenburg#text: The already retired Prussian general was recalled to service in 1914 and, after the victory over the Russian army at Tannenberg, was revered as the savior of East Prussia. From August 1916 he led the Supreme Army Command together with Erich Ludendorff, which in effect determined the policy of the Reich, and after the defeat he claimed before the Reichstag committee of inquiry that the army had been stabbed in the back, which lent authority to the stab-in-the-back legend. In 1925 the monarchist was elected Reich president of the republic and in 1932 reelected against Hitler. From 1930 he governed by emergency decrees and presidential cabinets, and on January 30, 1933, at the urging of his advisers, he appointed Hitler chancellor; he died in August 1934, whereupon Hitler seized the presidential office for himself.
gustav-stresemann#role: Chancellor and foreign minister of the Weimar Republic
gustav-stresemann#summary: Ended hyperinflation in 1923 and led Germany back into European politics with Locarno and membership in the League of Nations.
gustav-stresemann#text: The Berlin manufacturer's son and chairman of the liberal German People's Party had been a supporter of annexations during the war and after 1918 turned into a republican by reason. As chancellor he ended the Ruhr struggle in the autumn of 1923, put down communist and right-wing attempts at overthrow, and stabilized the currency with the Rentenmark. As foreign minister from 1923 to 1929 he relied on understanding with the victorious powers: the Dawes Plan regulated reparations, in the Treaties of Locarno of 1925 Germany recognized its western border, and in 1926 it joined the League of Nations. For this policy Stresemann received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1926 together with the French foreign minister Aristide Briand. His early death in October 1929, a few weeks before the stock market crash, robbed the republic of its ablest statesman.
friedrich-ebert#role: First Reich president of the Weimar Republic
friedrich-ebert#summary: Led Germany through the revolution of 1918 into parliamentary democracy and became its first head of state in 1919.
friedrich-ebert#text: The trained saddler from Heidelberg rose in the Social Democratic Party from union official to party chairman. On November 9, 1918, the last imperial chancellor Max von Baden handed the business of government over to him; as chairman of the Council of People's Deputies, Ebert steered toward elections to a national assembly rather than toward a council republic, and for this allied himself with the old army leadership and the Freikorps, which the left wing of the labor movement never forgave him. In February 1919 the national assembly elected him Reich president. During his term in office he fended off the Kapp Putsch, communist uprisings, and Hitler's putsch, and endured a flood of libel suits from the right. He died in 1925 at the age of 54 from a neglected case of appendicitis.
kaethe-kollwitz#summary: The most important German woman artist of her time gave lasting form to the suffering of mothers, workers, and victims of war.
kaethe-kollwitz#text: Käthe Kollwitz, born in Königsberg, lived as a physician's wife in the Berlin working-class district of Prenzlauer Berg and became famous for her etching cycles on the weavers' revolt and the Peasants' War. The death of her son Peter, who fell in Flanders in October 1914 as a war volunteer, made her a pacifist; her poster Never Again War of 1924 and the Grieving Parents at the Vladslo military cemetery of 1932 are among the most powerful works against war. In 1919 she became the first woman admitted to the Prussian Academy of Arts. In 1933 the National Socialists forced her to resign and banned her from exhibiting. She died in April 1945, a few weeks before the end of the war, in Moritzburg near Dresden.
marie-juchacz#role: Social Democratic politician and founder of the Workers' Welfare Association
marie-juchacz#summary: In 1919 she became the first woman to give a speech in a German parliament and built up the Workers' Welfare Association.
marie-juchacz#text: The daughter of a carpenter from Landsberg an der Warthe worked as a maid, factory worker, and seamstress before becoming active in the Social Democratic Party and taking charge of the party's women's work in 1917. On February 19, 1919, she stepped up to the lectern in the Weimar National Assembly and began with the words Gentlemen and ladies, which caused amusement; she declared that women did not give thanks for the right to vote, since it had been granted to them as a matter of course. In December 1919 she founded the Workers' Welfare Association, which supported the needy with children's homes, sewing rooms, and advice centers, and she sat in the Reichstag until 1933. She fled from the National Socialists by way of the Saarland and France to the United States, returned in 1949, and became honorary chairwoman of the Workers' Welfare Association.
albert-einstein#role: Physicist and founder of the theory of relativity
albert-einstein#summary: Revolutionized the understanding of space, time, and gravity and became the world's most famous scientist in 1919.
albert-einstein#text: Born in Ulm, Einstein published the special theory of relativity in 1905 as an employee of the Bern patent office, with the formula E equals m times c squared, and in 1915 completed in Berlin the general theory of relativity, which explains gravity as the curvature of space and time. When a British expedition measured during a solar eclipse in 1919 the deflection of starlight by the sun that he had predicted, he became world-famous overnight; in 1921 he received the Nobel Prize for the explanation of the photoelectric effect. Einstein was a convinced pacifist, signed a statement in 1914 against the war enthusiasm of his colleagues, and campaigned for democracy and understanding among nations, for which nationalists and antisemites attacked him. In 1933 he did not return to Germany and taught in Princeton until his death.
chiang-kai-shek#role: Chinese general and leader of the Nationalist Party Kuomintang
chiang-kai-shek#summary: Unified China under nationalist rule in 1928, fought communists and the Japanese, and lost the civil war in 1949.
chiang-kai-shek#text: Trained as an officer in Japan, he took over the leadership of the Nationalist Party, the Kuomintang, after Sun Yat-sen's death in 1925 and subdued the warlords who had ruled China since the fall of the empire in the Northern Expedition of 1926 to 1928. In 1927 he broke bloodily with the communists who had been his allies and governed from Nanjing a country he sought to modernize with German military aid and reforms. His campaigns against the communist bases set off the Long March in 1934; only after being kidnapped by his own generals at Xi'an in 1936 did he agree to a united front against Japan, which began open war in 1937. After the victory over Japan he lost to Mao Zedong in 1949 and fled to Taiwan, which he ruled autocratically until his death in 1975.
gilgamesch#role: Legendary king of Uruk (not historically confirmed)
gilgamesch#summary: Hero of the oldest epic in world literature, said to have built the city wall as king of Uruk and to have searched in vain for immortality.
gilgamesch#text: The Sumerian King List names Gilgamesh as the fifth king of the first dynasty of Uruk, who may have lived around 2700 BC; whether he really existed is not certain. In tradition he is two-thirds god and one-third human, a mighty and at first tyrannical ruler transformed by his friendship with the wild Enkidu. After Enkidu's death he seeks out Utnapishtim, the hero of the flood, to learn the secret of eternal life, and must recognize that immortality is denied to human beings. His story was told and copied in Mesopotamia for more than 2,000 years.
enheduanna#summary: Daughter of Sargon of Akkad and the first author known by name in world history.
enheduanna#text: Sargon of Akkad installed his daughter Enheduanna as high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur, the most important temple of Sumer, in order to bind the conquered cities to his empire. She composed hymns to the goddess Inanna and a collection of temple hymns in which she names herself as the author, which makes her the first poet in the world known by name. In one of her hymns she describes how she was driven from her office during a revolt and called on Inanna for help. An alabaster disk from Ur shows her at a sacrifice; her texts were still being copied in scribal schools centuries later.
ahmose-i#role: Pharaoh and founder of the New Kingdom
ahmose-i#summary: Drove the Hyksos out of Egypt and founded the Eighteenth Dynasty and the New Kingdom.
ahmose-i#text: Ahmose came from Thebes, where his family had already fought the Hyksos in the Nile Delta under his father and brother; his mother Ahhotep governed during his childhood. Around 1550 BC he captured the Hyksos capital Avaris, pursued his opponents as far as Palestine and restored control over Nubia. He reorganized the administration and the temples and had the last royal pyramid of Egypt built at Abydos. With him began the New Kingdom, the age of Hatshepsut, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ramesses II, in which Egypt became the great power of the Near East.
nofretete#summary: Great royal wife of Akhenaten, whose bust is among the most famous works of art in the world.
nofretete#text: Nefertiti, whose name means the beautiful one has come, was the principal wife of the pharaoh Akhenaten and the mother of six daughters. In the art of the Amarna period she appears unusually equal alongside the king: making offerings to the sun god Aten, on a chariot and even striking down enemies, an image otherwise reserved for the pharaoh. Some researchers suspect that she briefly reigned as pharaoh herself after Akhenaten's death. Her painted limestone bust was found in 1912 by Ludwig Borchardt in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose at Amarna and can be seen today in the Neues Museum in Berlin; Egypt demands its return.
tutanchamun#summary: The boy king who restored the old gods and became world famous through his tomb, discovered intact in 1922.
tutanchamun#text: Tutankhamun, probably a son of Akhenaten, came to the throne at about nine years of age. Under the influence of his advisers Ay and Horemheb he abandoned the cult of Aten, changed his name from Tutankhaten and restored the worship of Amun and the old capital Thebes. He died at about 18; examinations of his mummy point to malaria and a broken leg. His small tomb in the Valley of the Kings was almost untouched by robbers and was discovered in 1922 by Howard Carter. More than 5,000 grave goods, among them the golden death mask, chariots and thrones, made this insignificant king the best known pharaoh of all.
fu-hao#role: Queen, military commander and priestess of the Shang dynasty
fu-hao#summary: Consort of the Shang king Wu Ding who led armies into battle and whose undisturbed tomb was discovered in 1976.
fu-hao#text: Fu Hao was one of the wives of King Wu Ding, who ruled the Shang realm on the Yellow River from about 1250 to 1192 BC. Oracle bones record that she campaigned against neighboring peoples with as many as 13,000 soldiers, led sacrificial ceremonies and held land and a following of her own, which was extraordinary for a woman of her time. Wu Ding anxiously consulted the oracles about her health and her childbirths. Her tomb at Anyang, the only unplundered royal tomb of the Shang period, contained more than 400 bronze vessels, 750 jade objects, weapons, thousands of cowrie shells used as money and 16 human sacrifices, and makes her the best known figure of early China.
tiglat-pileser-i#summary: Made Assyria a great power for the first time at the end of the Bronze Age and reached the Mediterranean with his campaigns.
tiglat-pileser-i#text: Tiglath-Pileser I ruled from 1114 to 1076 BC, at a time when many kingdoms of the Near East had collapsed. He defeated the Mushki in Anatolia, subdued tribes in the northern mountains and marched to the Phoenician coast, where he received tribute from Byblos, Sidon and Arwad and reportedly hunted a dolphin. His inscriptions boast of hundreds of lions and elephants killed, and he had gardens with foreign trees laid out in Assur and a library built up. Under his successors Assyria lost power again, but his campaigns pointed the way for the later Neo-Assyrian Empire.
charles-darwin#summary: Founder of the theory of evolution by natural selection.
charles-darwin#text: From 1831 to 1836, Darwin sailed around the world as a young naturalist on the survey ship Beagle and gathered observations in the Galapagos Islands and South America that made him doubt the immutability of species. For more than two decades he tested his theory before publishing it in 1859, pressed by Alfred Russel Wallace, who had independently reached similar conclusions. In The Descent of Man he applied evolution to human beings as well in 1871. He was buried in Westminster Abbey.
florence-nightingale#summary: Founder of modern nursing and a pioneer of health statistics.
florence-nightingale#text: Against the will of her wealthy family, Nightingale trained as a nurse. In the Crimean War she took charge of the British military hospital at Scutari near Constantinople from 1854, where more soldiers died of disease than of wounds; through hygiene, clean linen and better nutrition she cut the death rate drastically. With vivid diagrams she convinced Parliament to reform the army medical service. The Nightingale School founded in London in 1860 made nursing a respected profession for women.
henry-dunant#summary: Founder of the Red Cross and the first recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize.
henry-dunant#text: The Geneva merchant Dunant happened upon the aftermath of the Battle of Solferino in northern Italy in 1859 and organized villagers to care for thousands of wounded men from both sides. His account of it led to the founding of the Red Cross in 1863 and to the Geneva Convention in 1864. Business failures left him impoverished, he was pushed out of the committee and lived forgotten for decades in a poorhouse in Heiden. In 1901 he received the first Nobel Peace Prize together with Frédéric Passy.
thomas-edison#summary: Developed the phonograph, the light bulb and the first electricity grid, and founded industrial research.
thomas-edison#text: Edison, who as a child attended school for only a few months and worked as a telegraph operator, set up the first industrial research laboratory at Menlo Park in 1876, where teams of mechanics and scientists developed inventions systematically. In 1877 he presented the phonograph, in 1879 a durable carbon filament light bulb and in 1882 the first public power station in New York. With more than 1,000 patents and companies such as General Electric he became the symbol of American inventiveness. In the struggle over direct or alternating current, however, he lost to Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse.
cecil-rhodes#role: British diamond magnate and colonial politician
cecil-rhodes#summary: Embodied British imperialism in Africa and founded the colony of Rhodesia.
cecil-rhodes#text: Rhodes came to South Africa in 1870 as the sickly son of a clergyman and built a monopoly on diamond mining with the firm De Beers within two decades. As prime minister of the Cape Colony from 1890 to 1896 he restricted the rights of the Black population, and his British South Africa Company conquered by force the territory of today's Zimbabwe and Zambia, which was named Rhodesia after him. His dream was a British railway from the Cape to Cairo. His fortune still funds the Rhodes Scholarships at Oxford; his monuments have been the target of protests against the colonial legacy since 2015.
bertha-von-suttner#summary: Author of the novel Lay Down Your Arms! and the first woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
bertha-von-suttner#text: Born in Prague as Countess Kinsky, she worked briefly as a secretary for Alfred Nobel in Paris in 1876 and remained in correspondence with him for the rest of her life. Her 1889 novel Lay Down Your Arms! depicted war from the perspective of a woman who loses her husband and relatives, and it was translated into many languages. In 1891 she founded the Austrian Peace Society, campaigned at international congresses for arbitration courts and disarmament, and convinced Nobel to endow a peace prize. In 1905 she received it herself; she died a few weeks before the outbreak of the World War she had warned against.
emmeline-pankhurst#summary: Leader of the militant suffragettes in the fight for women's suffrage in Britain.
emmeline-pankhurst#text: In 1903 Pankhurst founded the Women's Social and Political Union in Manchester, whose members became known as suffragettes. Since petitions and meetings achieved nothing, they turned to disruptions in Parliament, broken windows and arson attacks on empty buildings; Pankhurst was arrested repeatedly and went on hunger strike in prison, whereupon she was force-fed. In the First World War she suspended the campaign and supported the war effort. In 1918 British women over 30 received the vote, and in 1928, a few weeks after her death, it was made equal to that of men.
aischa-bint-abi-bakr#role: Wife of Muhammad and transmitter of hadith
aischa-bint-abi-bakr#summary: The daughter of the first caliph, regarded as the most important witness to the life of Muhammad, who exercised great influence in the community.
aischa-bint-abi-bakr#text: Aisha was the daughter of Abu Bakr, Muhammad's closest companion and later the first caliph, and was married to the Prophet at a young age; tradition holds that he valued her especially. After his death in 632 she lived for more than four decades in Medina, where scholars consulted her on questions of faith, law and daily life; more than 2,000 hadith, transmitted sayings and actions of Muhammad, go back to her testimony. In 656 she took a stand against the caliph Ali in the dispute over the succession and lost the Battle of the Camel near Basra against him, after which she withdrew from politics. For Sunnis she is a Mother of the Believers and one of the most significant scholars of the first generation; in Shiite Islam her role is viewed more critically because of the conflict with Ali.
al-chwarizmi#summary: The scholar at the House of Wisdom whose books of calculation gave algebra its name and carried the Indian numerals into the world.
al-chwarizmi#text: As his name says, al-Khwarizmi came from Khwarezm on the Aral Sea in present-day Uzbekistan and worked under the caliph al-Mamun in Baghdad. His book on calculation by completion and balancing was the first systematic textbook for solving equations and was translated into Latin in the 12th century; the word algebra comes from its title and the word algorithm from his name. He was the first in the Arab world to explain the place-value system with the ten Indian numerals in detail, calculated tables of the sun, moon and planets, and helped direct the measurement of the Earth's circumference. In his work of geography he improved the maps of Ptolemy for the Islamic world.
fatima-al-fihri#role: Founder of the al-Qarawiyyin mosque and school in Fez
fatima-al-fihri#summary: The merchant's daughter who used her inheritance to found a mosque in Fez in 859, from which one of the oldest universities in the world grew.
